:::{#thm-linearity-expectation}
#### Linearity of expectation

For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with defined expectations,
and constants $a$, $b$, and $c$:

$$\E{aX + bY + c} = a\E{X} + b\E{Y} + c$$

:::

::: proof

We prove the discrete case, applying @thm-lotus to the pair $(X, Y)$,
which is a single discrete random object with values $(x, y)$,
and $g(x, y) = ax + by + c$:

$$
\ba
\E{aX + bY + c}
&= \sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} (ax + by + c) \cd \P(X=x, Y=y)
&& \text{(LOTUS for the pair } (X, Y) \text{)}\\
&= a\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} x \cd \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + b\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \cd \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + c\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \P(X=x, Y=y)
&& \text{(distribute the sum over the terms; constants factor out)}\\
&= a\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} x \cd \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + b\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}}\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} y \cd \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + c\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \P(X=x, Y=y)
&& \text{(exchange the order of summation in the second term)}\\
&= a\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} x \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + b\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + c \cd 1
&& \text{(factor } x \text{ and } y \text{ out of the inner sums; total probability is 1)}\\
&= a\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} x \cd \P(X=x) + b\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \cd \P(Y=y) + c
&& \text{(marginalize: countable additivity)}\\
&= a\E{X} + b\E{Y} + c
&& \text{(definition of expectation)}
\ea
$$

Splitting and exchanging the sums is valid because the sums converge absolutely,
since $\abs{ax + by + c} \le \abs{a}\abs{x} + \abs{b}\abs{y} + \abs{c}$
and $\E{X}$ and $\E{Y}$ are defined.

Beyond the discrete case, this proof does not carry over by replacing sums with integrals.
That replacement would need a joint density for $(X, Y)$,
and some pairs have none:
if $X$ is continuous, the pair $(X, X)$ has no joint density.
In general, expectation is an integral against the probability measure,
and the theorem is the linearity of that (Lebesgue) integral
[@billingsley1995probability],
which is beyond these notes' scope.

:::
